chunks: 29 - From him, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from Muḥammad ibn al-Fuḍayl al-Kūfī, from Saʿd ibn Abī ʿAmr al-Jallāb, who said:

I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The two rakʿahs of al-fajr pass me by; should I perform them? He said: “Yes.” I said: Why? Are they obligatory? He said: “The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله instituted them as sunnah, so whatever the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله instituted is an obligation.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: His statement عليه السلام, “Whatever the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله instituted is an obligation,” means that it is determined, because the meaning of farḍ is determination. He does not mean that it is an obligation such that the one who abandons it deserves punishment. What indicates what we have said is what he narrated:

key_terms.أَفَأُصَلِّيهِمَا: should I perform the two prayers after missing them
key_terms.رَكْعَتَا الْفَجْرِ: the two units of prayer associated with fajr
key_terms.سَنَّهُمَا: he instituted them as sunnah (prophetic practice)
key_terms.فَرْضٌ: here, something established or determined, not necessarily punishable if omitted

ai.seo_question: If the two rakʿahs of fajr are missed, can they still be performed, and are they considered obligatory?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the two rakʿahs of fajr and affirms that they may be performed if missed. It also explains that the term farḍ here does not mean a duty whose omission incurs punishment, but rather something established and determined through the sunnah of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله.
